title: The two birds again; the swan in the wheel (1.6)
hook: a swan wanders the great wheel, lost as long as it thinks it is separate from the one who turns it

segments.voice: Yesterday: the wheel, one rim, three tires, fifty spokes, all turning around a hub that barely moves. Did you catch yourself on a spoke, and see the wheel around it? Today, a bird inside that wheel. Day four hundred twenty-three.

Six days ago, in the Mundaka, you met two birds on one tree. One eats the fruit, sweet and bitter. The other doesn't eat. It just watches. Here's the surprise: the Shvetashvatara tells that story again, almost word for word, in its fourth chapter. Two Upanishads, the same two birds. But before it gets there, in its very first chapter, this text has already put a different bird to work. Not on a tree this time. On the wheel.
screen: `TWO BIRDS, ONE TREE.` → `THE SAME VERSE, IN A SECOND UPANISHAD.` → `A NEW BIRD, ON THE WHEEL.`

segments.voice: Verse 1.6 goes like this, in paraphrase. In this huge wheel of Brahman, which lives in everything and holds everything, the swan wanders around and around, as long as it thinks that itself and the one who moves it are two different things. When it is blessed by that one, it reaches what does not die. The Sanskrit word is hamsa, swan or wild goose. In Hindu teaching the hamsa became a picture of the soul: a bird that flies high, crosses great distances, and, tradition says, rests on water without getting wet. Put that bird inside yesterday's wheel. It flies spoke to spoke, life to life, mood to mood, and it never lands. Why? Not because the wheel is evil. Because of a thought: I am out here, and the one who turns all this is somewhere else. That is what keeps it circling. Now hear the two birds again, from chapter four. One bird eats and grieves, confused, until it sees the other, the Lord, and its glory, and then its grief falls away. Same move. The lost bird isn't fixed by flying harder. It is freed by seeing who has been there all along. And notice one word that is new here: blessed. Here the Shvetashvatara makes grace part of the turn. The swan doesn't just figure it out. It is helped home. Scholars and teachers read that sentence in different ways: Advaita teachers as the self recognizing it was never separate, devotional schools as a soul brought close by a loving Lord.
screen: `THE SWAN CIRCLES THE WHEEL.` · `LOST WHILE IT THINKS: WE ARE TWO.` · `THE TWO BIRDS, TOLD AGAIN.` · then, large: `BLESSED, IT COMES HOME.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the body settle. Picture a white bird, flying in slow circles. Each circle is one thing you're busy with today. Let it fly a few rounds. Then imagine it coming down onto still water, wings folding, not even wet. Let your breath be the water. Whenever a thought lifts you off again, notice it, and let the bird come back down. If you pray, you might rest in the thought of the one the verse says turns the wheel. The bell holds the time.
Hamsa, a swan. The Shvetashvatara retells the Mundaka's two birds, and adds the hamsa that circles the wheel until it stops thinking it stands apart.

Your line: the swan. When you notice yourself circling today, the same worry for the tenth time, picture the swan landing on still water, and take one slow breath before you fly again. Day four hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: The hamsa appears as an image of the soul in Hindu songs and teaching, and Paramahamsa, 'highest swan', is a title given to some renunciates; teachers pair the swan of 1.6 with the two birds of Mundaka 3.1 and Shvetashvatara 4.6–4.7.

myth: the two birds appear in only one Upanishad
they appear in the Mundaka (3.1) and again in the Shvetashvatara (4.6–4.7).
the swan circles because it thinks it and the mover are two
verse 1.6 names that thought as what keeps it wandering.
in verse 1.6 the swan gets free entirely by its own effort
the verse says it reaches the deathless when it is blessed, or favored, by the one who moves the wheel.

fork.setup: you're the swan, flying circle after circle inside the great wheel. what brings you home, according to the verse?
options: fly faster, until you reach the rim.
stop thinking you and the mover are two, and be met by grace.
leave the wheel and find another one.
fork.reveal: the swan wanders while it thinks it and the mover are separate. favored by that one, it reaches what does not die.

original.note: Sanskrit haṃsa: swan or wild goose. in 1.6 the soul that circles the wheel of Brahman.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty bird in a poem.
what it means: the soul, flying round the wheel of lives, until it stops seeing itself as apart from the one who turns it.
what a scholar hears: 1.6 joins knowledge and grace (the swan is 'favored' by the mover), a pairing that runs through the Shvetashvatara and that devotional schools later build on.

sources.ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.6 (the swan in the wheel of Brahman)

notes: 'Six days ago' refers to day 417 (Mundaka's two birds). Confirm if the sequence changes.
Hamsa as an image of the soul, landing on water without getting wet: widely used in later devotional and yogic imagery; the 'unwetted' detail is traditional, not from this verse.
Reading of 'jushtas tatas tena' as 'blessed/favored by him': confirm rendering; Advaita and theistic readings are both mentioned without ranking.
